'''Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal''' (4 March 1931 – 8 May 2011) was an Indian reproductive biologist, [[endocrinologist]] and the chairman of the Department of Biochemistry and dean of Faculty of Science at the [[Indian Institute of Science]]. He was known for his pioneering researches on [[gonadotropin]] and was an elected fellow of the [[Indian Academy of Sciences]] and the [[Indian National Science Academy]]. He was an associate of noted scientists, [[Choh Hao Li]] and [[Rodney Robert Porter]] and discovered the role of hormones in generating immune response in living beings, during his association with the former. The [[Council of Scientific and Industrial Research]], the apex agency of the Government of India for scientific research, awarded him the [[Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize for Science and Technology]], one of the highest Indian science awards for his contributions to Medical Sciences in 1976.

== Biography ==
[[File:Crawford Hall, University of Mysore.jpg|thumb|left|Crawford Hall, University of Mysore]]
[[File:IISc Admin Building.jpg|thumb|Indian Institute of Science]]
Raghuveer Moudgal was born on 4 March 1931<ref name="Fellow profile">{{Cite web |url=http://www.ias.ac.in/describe/fellow/Moudgal,_Prof._Nuggehalli_Raghuveer |title=Fellow profile |date=2016 |publisher=Indian Academy of Sciences}}</ref> in [[Mysore]], in the south Indian state of [[Karnataka]], in a Hindu family to Vaidehi, a homemaker and N. Narasimha Moudgal, an electrical engineer with the State Electricity Board who reportedly contributed significantly to the electrification of the erstwhile [[Mysore state]].<ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches">{{Cite journal |last1=Rao |first1=AJ |last2=Rao |first2=Appaji |year=2012 |title=NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches |url=http://www.ias.ac.in/article/fulltext/jbsc/037/02/0207-0210 |journal=Journal of Biosciences |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=207–10 |doi=10.1007/s12038-012-9207-5 |pmid=22581325|s2cid=35048530 }}</ref> He was the youngest of their three boys and two girls.{{Refn|group=note|His brothers were N. Shyam Prasad and N. Ram Prasad while Prabha Devi Anantram and Harini Madhava Rao were his sisters.}} His early schooling was at Seshadripuram High School, [[Bengaluru]] where he passed the matriculation in 1946.  He moved to [[Kolhapur]] to complete his graduate studies at the [[University of Bombay]] in 1950, staying at his elder sister's house.<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir">{{Cite journal |last=Kambadur Muralidhar |title=Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal – Biographical Memoir |url=http://www.insaindia.res.in/BM/BM40_1304.pdf |publisher=Indian National Science Academy |date=2013 |volume=40 |pages=57–74}}</ref> Opting for a research degree for his post graduate studies, he joined the [[University of Madras]] and earned an MSc for his researches on the biochemistry of [[thyroid hormones]]. Continuing in [[Chennai]],{{Refn|group=note|Chennai was then known as Madras}} he pursued his doctoral studies under the guidance of P. S. Sarma, a noted biochemist, and secured a PhD in 1957. He went to the [[University of California, Berkeley]] in the US for his post-doctoral studies and worked as a post-doctoral fellow at the laboratory of [[Choh Hao Li]], a Chinese-born US biochemist who would later describe the structure of [[somatotropin]], a pituitary growth hormone.<ref name="Choh Hao Li">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/li-choh-h.pdf |title=Choh Hao Li |last=R. David Cole |date=2017 |publisher=National Academy of Sciences}}</ref>

In 1961, he moved out of the US to continue his post-doctoral work in the UK at [[St Mary's Hospital Medical School]], London on a [[Wellcome Trust]] fellowship.<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal (1931–2011)">{{Cite web |url=http://www.currentscience.ac.in/Volumes/101/01/0109.pdf |title=Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal (1931–2011) |date=2011 |publisher=Current Science |pages=109–110}}</ref> There, he joined the wards of [[Rodney Robert Porter]], [[List of Nobel laureates in Physiology or Medicine|Nobel laureate]] biochemist,{{Refn|group=note|Porter shared the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] with [[Gerald Edelman]] in 1972.<ref name="The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1972">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1972/index.html |title=The Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 1972 |date=2017 |publisher=Nobelprize.org}}</ref>}} and spent a year at Porter's laboratory. On his return to India, he joined the [[All India Institute of Medical Sciences, Delhi]] as a [[Council of Scientific and Industrial Research|CSIR]] Pool Officer. It was during this period his doctoral adviser, P. S. Sarma, invited him to join the [[Indian Institute of Science]] (IISc) as an assistant professor. At IISc, he continued his researches with the assistance of a grant from [[Ford Foundation]] and in 1969 he received an invitation from R. O. Greep of [[Harvard University]] for collaborative research.<ref name="Commentary">{{Cite web |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/224950573 |title=Commentary |date=2012 }}</ref> Moudgal stayed at Harvard for two years to supervise the work of Greep's Group and returned to IISc in 1971. He based his subsequent researches at the institute, simultaneously working as an associate professor and later as a professor. At the time of his retirement from official service in 1993, he was holding the positions of the Chairman of the Department of Biochemistry and the Dean of the Science Faculty.<ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches" /> Post retirement, he continued to be associated with IISc as an [[Indian National Science Academy|INSA]] senior scientist and an honorary professor.<ref name="Deceased fellow - Moudgal">{{Cite web |url=http://insaindia.res.in/detail/N79-0482 |title=Deceased fellow – Moudgal |date=2016 |publisher=Indian National Science Academy |access-date=2017-10-22 |archive-date=22 October 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171022193650/http://insaindia.res.in/detail/N79-0482 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="Frontiers in Bioscience : Editors">{{Cite web |url=http://bio-mirror.im.ac.cn/mirrors/bioscience/editmemb/moudgal.htm |title=Frontiers in Bioscience : Editors |date=2017 |publisher=Frontiers in Bioscience |access-date=22 February 2017 |archive-date=23 February 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170223041410/http://bio-mirror.im.ac.cn/mirrors/bioscience/editmemb/moudgal.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Moudgal was pursuing his doctoral studies at Madras University when he married Biligiri Rao née Prapulla in 1957.<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir" /> The couple had two sons, Pradeep and Madan, and a daughter, Priya. Towards the later part of his life, he suffered from cancer and underwent treatment in the US. He succumbed to the disease on 8 May 2011, at a hospital in [[Dublin, California]], survived by his children, their spouses and grandchildren; his wife predeceased him in 2008.<ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches" />

== Legacy ==
[[File:Steroidogenesis.svg|235px|thumb|Steroidogenesis]]
[[File:Cute Monkey cropped.jpg|thumb|left|Bonnet macaque]]
Moudgal's early researches at the University of Madras were on the biochemistry of thyroid hormones but he shifted his focus to [[pituitary]] [[gonadotropins]] during his days at Choh Hao Li's laboratory at the University of California, Berkeley when he established that the hormones generated [[Immunogenicity|immune response]] in living beings and the discovery was reported to be a significant one as the belief till then was the principal function of the hormones was [[reproduction]].<ref name="Commentary" /> Later, at Rodney Porter's laboratory in London, he worked on the role of [[cellulose]] as a carrier for immobilization of antibodies. Back in India, he expanded the scope of his researches to cover wider aspects of [[reproductive biology]] for which he established a Primate Research Laboratory at IISc in 1965, which was the largest [[primate]] house in the country at that time.<ref name="Deceased fellow - Moudgal" /><ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches" /> Working on the macaques in his primate house, he discovered that [[sialidase]] from the kidney of the primate acted as an inhibitor of [[follicle stimulating hormone]] (FSH), a hormone responsible for pubertal development.<ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches" /> He conducted elaborate studies on the molecular mechanism of [[Luteinizing Hormone]] (LH), a hormone which has significant role in [[ovulation]] and [[testosterone]] production, and elucidated the ''unfolding of LH binding to LH receptors in the target cell''<ref name="Brief Profile of the Awardee">{{Cite web |url=http://ssbprize.gov.in/content/Detail.aspx?AID=194 |title=Brief Profile of the Awardee |date=2017 |publisher=Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize}}</ref><ref name="Handbook of Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize Winners">{{cite web | url=http://www.csirhrdg.res.in/ssb.pdf | title=Handbook of Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize Winners | publisher=Council of Scientific and Industrial Research | date=1999 | access-date=22 February 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304043957/http://www.csirhrdg.res.in/ssb.pdf | archive-date=4 March 2016 | url-status=dead }}</ref> which was detailed in one of his articles, ''Effect of ICSH on Early Pregnancy in Hypophysectomized Pregnant Rats'', published in Nature in 1969.<ref name="Effect of ICSH on Early Pregnancy in Hypophysectomized Pregnant Rats">{{cite journal |doi=10.1038/222286a0 |pmid=5778402 |title=Effect of ICSH on Early Pregnancy in Hypophysectomized Pregnant Rats |journal=Nature |volume=222 |issue=5190 |pages=286–7 |year=1969 |last1=Moudgal |first1=N. R. |bibcode=1969Natur.222..286M |s2cid=4251088 }}</ref> He discovered that neutralizing LH resulted in neutralization of several reproductive functions such as ovulation, implantation, and gestational progress and the discovery opened a new methodology in immunocontraceptive technology.<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir" /> Later, he furthered his investigations on hormone actions by using antibodies as probes. His findings reportedly prompted R. O. Greep of Harvard University to invite him for collaborative research and Moudgal supervised the work of Greep's Group at his laboratory. At Harvard, he also collaborated with W. R. Moyle and established the presence of [[Luteinizing hormone/choriogonadotropin receptor]]s on tumor cells in the testicles for the first time, which they revealed in an article, ''Specific binding of luteinizing hormone to Leydig tumor cells'', published in the ''[[Journal of Biological Chemistry]]'' in 1971.<ref name="Specific binding of luteinizing hormone to Leydig tumor cells">{{cite journal |pmid=5570432 |year=1971 |last1=Moudgal |first1=N. R. |title=Specific binding of luteinizing hormone to Leydig tumor cells |journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry |volume=246 |issue=16 |pages=4983–6 |last2=Moyle |first2=W. R. |last3=Greep |first3=R. O. |doi=10.1016/S0021-9258(18)61960-X |doi-access=free }}</ref> He used these tumor cells for further investigations on Hormone-Receptor interactions, [[Cyclic adenosine monophosphate]] (cyclic AMP) production and [[steroidogenesis]] and experimentally demonstrated the extent of coupling and response with regard to cyclic AMP production and steroid output.<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir" />{{Refn|group=note|[[Earl Wilbur Sutherland Jr.]] won the [[Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine]] in 1971 for his discovery of cyclic AMP as secondary messengers.<ref name="Earl W. Sutherland, Jr. - Facts">{{Cite web |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/medicine/laureates/1971/sutherland-facts.html |title=Earl W. Sutherland, Jr. – Facts |date=2017 |publisher=Nobelprize.org}}</ref>}}

[[Bonnet macaque]]s raised by him at Primate Research Laboratory{{Refn|group=note|The laboratory housed around 400 primates.}} made it handy for Moudgal in carrying out researches on follicle stimulating hormone in the primates and he discovered that immuno-neutralization of circulating FSH decreases the [[semen]] count, leading to [[oligozoospermia]] or [[azoospermia]], but did not adversely affect [[libido]].<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir" /> He successfully replicated the experiments in rodents as well and suggested FSH as an [[Immunocontraception|immunocontraceptive]] protocol.<ref name="Death of Professor N. Raghuveer Moudgal">{{Cite web |url=http://www.ssr.org/sites/ssr.org/files/uploads/attachments/node/74/moudgal_obituary.pdf |title=Death of Professor N. Raghuveer Moudgal |date=2017 |publisher=Society for the Study of Reproduction |access-date=22 February 2017 |archive-date=21 May 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140521033632/http://www.ssr.org/sites/ssr.org/files/uploads/attachments/node/74/moudgal_obituary.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> However, the researches could not be furthered due to laws related to preparation of protein-based pharmaceuticals. Still, his studies widened the understanding of conditions such as follicular maturation, [[atresia]], [[spermatogenesis]], primate reproduction and [[lactational amenorrhea]]. The pioneering work carried out by him led to the Indian Council of Medical Research recognizing his laboratory at IISc as a Centre for Advanced Research in Reproductive Biology, which as since been upgraded as Department of Molecular Reproduction and Developmental Genetics (MRDG).<ref name="Commentary" /><ref name="Department of Molecular Reproduction and Developmental Genetics">{{Cite web |url=http://www.mrdg.iisc.ernet.in/ |title=Department of Molecular Reproduction and Developmental Genetics |date=2017 |publisher=Indian Institute of Science |access-date=22 February 2017 |archive-date=10 January 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200110120534/http://www.mrdg.iisc.ernet.in/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> He documented his researches by way of several articles<ref name="Moudgal NR[au] ">{{Cite web |url=https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed?cmd=search&term=Moudgal%20NR%5Bau%5D&dispmax=50 |title=Moudgal NR[au]  |date=2017 |publisher=PubMed}}</ref>{{Refn|group=note|Please see ''Selected bibliography'' section}} and his work has been cited by a number of authors and researchers.<ref name="Li2012">{{cite book|author=Choh Hao Li|title=Gonadotropic Hormones|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Sxt0PGXag-gC&pg=PA182|date=2 December 2012|publisher=Elsevier|isbn=978-0-323-16027-8|pages=182–}}</ref><ref Science|isbn=978-0-323-16126-8|pages=196–}}</ref>

== Professional associations ==
Moudgal, who was the secretary of the Society of Biological Chemists (India) from 1967 to 1969,<ref name="Secretaries">{{Cite web |url=http://www.iisc.ernet.in/sbci/images/sbc-rules%20(79%20Book).pdf |title=Secretaries |date=2017 |page=17 |publisher=Society of Biological Chemists (India) |access-date=22 February 2017 |archive-date=9 August 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200809130829/http://www.iisc.ernet.in/sbci/images/sbc-rules%20(79%20Book).pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> served as the secretary-general of the Federation of Asian and Oceanian Biochemists (FAOB) during 1972–75<ref name="Secretaries-General/Treasurers">{{Cite web |url=http://faobmb.com/about-faobmb/history-of-faobmb/ |title=Secretaries-General/Treasurers |date=2017 |publisher=Federation of Asian and Oceanian Biochemists (FAOB) }}</ref> and was a member of the Endocrine Society and the Society for the study of Reproduction, both US-based societies.<ref name="NR Moudgal – A pioneer in the development of immunocontraceptive approaches" /> He was one of the founders of the Indian Society for the Study of Reproduction and Fertility and served as its first president.<ref name="Commentary" /> He organized an International Symposium on gonadotropins which was attended by some of the major names in the field of reproductive biology including [[Malur R. Narasimha Prasad]], [[Gursaran Talwar]], [[Sardul Singh Guraya]], [[Fernand Labrie]] and [[Om P. Bahl]].<ref name="Nuggehalli Raghuveer Moudgal - Biographical Memoir" /> He was a member of the task force of the [[World Health Organization]] for research in human reproduction for a number of years,<ref name="Death of Professor N. Raghuveer Moudgal" /> sat in the editorial board of [[Molecular and Cellular Endocrinology]] and was the founding editor of ''[[Journal of Biosciences]]''.<ref name="Commentary" /> He also served as the editor of [[Frontiers in Bioscience]].<ref name="Editors listed in alphabetical order">{{Cite web |url=http://int-prop.lf2.cuni.cz/heart_sounds/h14/abdlist.htm |title=Editors listed in alphabetical order |date=2017 |publisher=Frontiers in Bioscience}}</ref>

|url=http://www.indnet.org/ias/Contents/Fellowship/Fellows/k-index.html |title=IAS fellowship |year=2017 |publisher=IndNet |access-date=22 February 2017 |archive-date=22 February 2017 Research]] awarded him [[Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize]], one of the highest Indian science awards in 1976.<ref name="Medical Sciences">{{Cite web |url=http://www.csir.res.in/external/heads/career/award/BPRIZE/Medical_SCIENCES.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130224074105/http://www.csir.res.in/External/Heads/career/award/BPRIZE/Medical_SCIENCES.htm |url-status=dead |archive-date=24 February 2013 |title=Medical
